10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: The foundational vocabulary of graph theory: a graph G=(V,E) consists of a set of nodes (vertices) V representing entities, and a set of edges E representing relationships/connections between pairs of nodes; an edge can be undirected (a symmetric relationship, like 'is friends with') or directed (an asymmetric relationship with a source and target, like 'follows' or 'cites').
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Graphs exist because many real-world systems are fundamentally relational - data points don't just have features, they have connections to other data points, and those connections often carry as much or more information than the node attributes themselves. The directed/undirected distinction exists because many real relationships are inherently asymmetric (A follows B doesn't imply B follows A; A cites B doesn't imply B cites A), and modeling this asymmetry correctly is essential - treating a directed graph as undirected discards information about direction of influence/flow.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: Formally, V is a set of nodes, and E is a set of pairs of nodes - for undirected graphs, E contains unordered pairs {u,v} (edge (u,v) is the same as (v,u)); for directed graphs, E contains ordered pairs (u,v) where u is the source and v is the target, and (u,v) is distinct from (v,u). Many real graphs are 'mixed' or can be represented either way depending on the question being asked - a citation network is naturally directed (paper A cites paper B), but you might convert it to undirected to study co-citation communities.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use directed graphs whenever the relationship has a clear source/target asymmetry with meaningfully different semantics in each direction (web links, citations, social media follows, transaction flows, dependency graphs); use undirected graphs when the relationship is inherently symmetric (mutual friendships, co-authorship, physical adjacency/proximity, molecular bonds).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't force a directed relationship into an undirected representation if direction matters for your downstream task (e.g., PageRank's notion of 'importance' depends critically on link direction - treating web links as undirected destroys the concept of authority flowing from linked-to pages); conversely, don't add artificial directionality to genuinely symmetric relationships, as it can confuse algorithms that assume edge symmetry (some GNN layers and graph algorithms assume undirected graphs by default).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: A common bug is loading a directed edge list but feeding it to an algorithm/library that assumes undirected graphs (or vice versa) without explicitly specifying the graph type - this silently changes results (e.g., an undirected PageRank computation on a citation graph gives different, often less meaningful, rankings than the directed version). Another common issue is inconsistent edge representation when converting between formats - some libraries store directed edges as both (u,v) and (v,u) to represent undirected graphs, and forgetting this convention when counting edges leads to double-counting.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: A citation network where edges point from citing paper to cited paper is directed - PageRank on this directed graph identifies influential 'foundational' papers (heavily cited, i.e., high in-degree from many sources); if you instead built an undirected 'co-citation' graph (edge between two papers if they're often cited together by the same third paper), you'd be answering a different question - which papers are topically related - using the same underlying citation data but a fundamentally different graph structure.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: Two standard data structures for representing a graph computationally: an adjacency matrix is an n×n matrix A where A[i][j] = 1 (or edge weight) if there's an edge from node i to node j and 0 otherwise; an adjacency list stores, for each node, a list of its neighbors (and optionally edge weights), typically as a dictionary/array of lists.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Graphs need a concrete in-memory representation before any algorithm can operate on them, and the choice of representation has major implications for memory usage and algorithm efficiency - the adjacency matrix and adjacency list exist as the two complementary standard choices, trading off between dense/matrix-friendly operations (useful for spectral methods, GNN message passing as matrix multiplication) and memory-efficient sparse representations (useful for the vast majority of real-world graphs, which are sparse).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: The adjacency matrix represents the full n×n connectivity structure explicitly - row i, column j indicates the edge (i,j); for undirected graphs the matrix is symmetric (A=A^T). This makes operations like 'is there an edge between i and j' O(1) and enables matrix-based algorithms (e.g., A^k gives counts of k-step paths, eigendecomposition gives spectral properties), but requires O(n^2) memory regardless of how many edges actually exist. The adjacency list represents only the edges that exist - for each node, a list of its neighbors - giving O(V+E) memory, ideal for sparse graphs (where E << V^2), but operations like 'is there an edge between i and j' require scanning a neighbor list (O(degree)) rather than O(1) lookup.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use adjacency lists for most real-world graph storage and traversal algorithms (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra) since real-world graphs (social networks, web graphs, molecules) are almost always sparse - a graph with millions of nodes but average degree of 10-100 would need petabytes for a dense adjacency matrix but only megabytes-to-gigabytes for an adjacency list. Use adjacency matrices (or sparse matrix formats like CSR/COO that are conceptually adjacency-list-like but enable matrix operations) when you need matrix algebra - spectral graph theory, GNN message passing implemented as sparse matrix multiplication (A @ X), or when the graph is genuinely dense/small.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Avoid dense adjacency matrices for large sparse graphs - a graph with 1 million nodes would require a matrix with 10^12 entries (8 TB as float64), even if there are only a few million actual edges; avoid adjacency lists when you need fast random-access edge-existence queries on a dense graph, where the matrix's O(1) lookup wins.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Naively constructing a dense adjacency matrix for a large real-world graph (common mistake when porting toy-example code to real data) causes out-of-memory errors or catastrophic slowdowns; conversely, using a pure Python adjacency list (list of lists) for matrix-heavy GNN computations is far slower than using sparse tensor formats (PyTorch's sparse tensors, scipy.sparse) that combine adjacency-list-like memory efficiency with matrix-operation APIs. Self-loops and multi-edges (multiple edges between the same pair of nodes) need explicit handling in both representations and are a common source of off-by-one or double-counting bugs.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: PyTorch Geometric represents graphs using an 'edge_index' tensor of shape [2, num_edges] - essentially a compact adjacency-list (COO sparse matrix) representation - because real molecular graphs, citation networks, and social graphs in PyG datasets have millions of nodes but are extremely sparse, making a dense adjacency matrix completely impractical; spectral GNN variants that need eigendecomposition instead operate on the sparse Laplacian matrix, computed without ever materializing a dense n×n matrix.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: The degree of a node is the number of edges incident to it - for undirected graphs, simply 'degree'; for directed graphs, split into in-degree (number of incoming edges) and out-degree (number of outgoing edges), since a node can receive many connections while sending few, or vice versa.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Degree is the most basic measure of a node's connectivity/importance in a graph, and exists as a building block for almost every higher-level graph concept - it's the simplest centrality measure, a key input to algorithms like PageRank (which normalizes by out-degree) and GCN (which normalizes aggregation by degree to prevent high-degree nodes from dominating), and the basis for understanding degree distributions (e.g., scale-free/power-law networks where a few 'hub' nodes have very high degree).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: For an undirected graph, degree(v) = number of edges touching v (a self-loop typically counts as 2, by convention, since it contributes to both 'ends'). For a directed graph, in-degree(v) = number of edges (u,v) pointing into v, and out-degree(v) = number of edges (v,u) pointing out of v; the sum of all in-degrees equals the sum of all out-degrees equals the total number of edges. The degree sequence (the sorted list of all node degrees) characterizes a graph's connectivity pattern - real-world networks typically have heavy-tailed degree distributions (most nodes have low degree, a few 'hubs' have very high degree), unlike random (Erdős–Rényi) graphs which have roughly uniform degree.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use degree as a quick, cheap first-pass measure of node importance/influence before reaching for more expensive centrality measures (betweenness, eigenvector centrality, PageRank); use in-degree specifically to find 'popular'/'authoritative' nodes in directed graphs (highly-cited papers, frequently-followed accounts) and out-degree to find 'active'/'broadcasting' nodes (prolific posters, hub routers); degree normalization (dividing by degree, or using degree in the denominator of aggregation) is essential in GNN message passing to prevent high-degree nodes from having disproportionately large-magnitude aggregated representations.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't use raw degree as a proxy for 'importance' in graphs where indirect/global connectivity matters more than direct connections - a node with low degree but connecting two otherwise-disconnected dense clusters (high betweenness) can be far more structurally important than a high-degree node within a single dense cluster; degree alone says nothing about WHO a node is connected to (a node connected to many low-importance nodes vs. a few high-importance nodes have very different 'true' importance, which eigenvector centrality/PageRank capture but raw degree doesn't).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to distinguish in-degree from out-degree in directed graphs leads to misinterpretation - e.g., treating Twitter 'follower count' (in-degree) and 'following count' (out-degree) as the same kind of signal when they have very different meanings (influence vs. activity); nodes with degree zero (isolated nodes) can cause division-by-zero errors in degree-normalized computations (PageRank, GCN normalization) if not handled with care (e.g., adding self-loops or epsilon smoothing).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: In a GCN layer, the symmetric normalization D^(-1/2) A D^(-1/2) (where D is the diagonal degree matrix) ensures that a node's aggregated neighbor representation isn't simply 'larger' for high-degree nodes - without this normalization, a celebrity account with millions of followers in a social graph would produce aggregated feature vectors with much larger magnitude purely due to summing over more neighbors, regardless of the actual information content, biasing the GNN's learned representations.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: A path is a sequence of nodes connected by edges with no repeated nodes (a walk that doesn't revisit nodes); a cycle is a path that returns to its starting node, forming a closed loop; a connected component is a maximal subset of nodes where every pair is reachable from each other via some path (for directed graphs, this generalizes to 'weakly connected' - ignoring direction - and 'strongly connected' - respecting direction - components).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: These concepts exist because 'is everything in my graph actually one connected thing, or several separate pieces?' and 'can I get from A to B, and how?' are among the most fundamental questions you can ask about a graph's structure, underlying tasks from network reachability analysis to fraud-ring detection to molecular ring-system identification (cycles in molecular graphs correspond to ring structures critical to chemical properties).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: Connected components are found via simple traversal (BFS/DFS from each unvisited node, marking all reachable nodes as one component) in O(V+E) time; for directed graphs, strongly connected components (SCCs - sets of nodes mutually reachable from each other respecting edge direction) require algorithms like Tarjan's or Kosaraju's, also O(V+E). Cycle detection uses DFS with a 'currently being visited' marker - if DFS encounters a node already on the current recursion stack, a cycle exists (this is also how dependency-graph 'circular dependency' detection works). A graph (or component) with no cycles is a tree (if connected) or forest (if disconnected).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use connected-component analysis to identify isolated subgraphs/clusters (e.g., separate social circles with no cross-connections, disconnected regions of a transportation network); use strongly-connected-component analysis on directed graphs to find groups of mutually-reachable nodes (e.g., in a citation network, an SCC would indicate a 'citation cycle' - unusual and possibly indicating citation rings); use cycle detection for dependency validation (build systems, package managers checking for circular dependencies) and for chemistry (identifying ring structures in molecules, which strongly influence molecular properties).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't run expensive global connectivity algorithms repeatedly on a graph that changes incrementally - if edges are added/removed dynamically, use incremental/dynamic connectivity data structures (union-find with online updates) rather than recomputing full BFS/DFS from scratch each time; cycle detection via naive DFS can be exponential if not properly marking visited nodes (a common bug in recursive implementations without memoization).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Confusing 'connected' (undirected reachability, or weak connectivity for directed graphs) with 'strongly connected' (directed reachability in both directions) leads to incorrect conclusions - e.g., a citation network might be weakly connected (everything reachable ignoring direction) but have very few or no large strongly-connected components (citation cycles are rare), and treating these as the same metric misrepresents the graph's structure; forgetting that real-world graphs often have one giant connected component plus many tiny isolated components (the 'giant component' phenomenon) can lead to mistakenly running algorithms on the whole graph when only the giant component is meaningful.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) is the standard algorithm for incrementally tracking connected components as edges are added - used in Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm and in fraud-detection systems that incrementally cluster transaction graphs into connected components (a sudden merge of two previously-separate components when a new transaction edge is added can flag a potential money-laundering link between previously-unrelated account clusters).

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: The eccentricity of a node v is the maximum shortest-path distance from v to any other node in the graph (how far the 'farthest' node is); the diameter of a graph is the maximum eccentricity over all nodes - i.e., the longest shortest-path distance between any pair of nodes (the 'worst-case' distance across the whole graph).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Diameter and eccentricity exist to quantify how 'spread out' or 'compact' a graph is - critical for understanding information/influence propagation speed (how many hops does it take for information to potentially reach everyone?), and famously relevant to the 'small-world' phenomenon (most real social networks have surprisingly small diameters - the 'six degrees of separation' idea - despite having millions of nodes), which has direct implications for GNN design (how many message-passing layers/hops are needed to let information flow across the whole graph).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: Computing exact diameter requires computing all-pairs shortest paths (via BFS from every node for unweighted graphs, O(V*(V+E)), or Floyd-Warshall O(V^3) for weighted graphs with possible negative edges) and taking the maximum - this is expensive for large graphs, so diameter is often estimated via sampling (BFS from a sample of nodes) or approximated via algorithms like HyperANF that use probabilistic counting. The related concept of 'average path length' (mean shortest-path distance over all pairs) is often more informative than diameter for large graphs, since diameter can be dominated by a few outlier long paths while most pairs are much closer.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use diameter/eccentricity to characterize a network's overall connectivity/compactness (comparing networks, detecting structural anomalies like an unusually long 'bridge' connecting otherwise-tight clusters); use the small-world insight to inform GNN architecture choices - if your graph has small diameter (most real social/citation networks do, often 4-8 hops), a GNN with that many message-passing layers can theoretically let any node's information reach any other node, motivating the number of layers chosen.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Avoid computing exact diameter on very large graphs (millions+ of nodes) via brute-force all-pairs shortest paths - use sampling-based approximations instead; don't over-interpret diameter for graphs with highly skewed degree distributions, where a single long 'chain' of low-degree nodes can dominate the diameter even though the 'core' of the graph (the densely-connected hub nodes) has a much smaller effective diameter.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Computing diameter on disconnected graphs without first restricting to a single connected component gives an infinite or undefined diameter (no path exists between components) - a common bug when working with real scraped network data that often has many small disconnected fragments alongside one giant component; assuming a graph's diameter directly tells you how many GNN layers you need can be misleading because over-smoothing (covered elsewhere) means very deep GNNs (matching large diameters) often perform worse, not better, in practice.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: The famous 'six degrees of separation' finding (and its empirical confirmation in the Facebook social graph, which found an average separation of about 3.5-4 'hops' between users) demonstrates the small-world property - despite having billions of nodes, the graph's effective diameter is tiny, which is why a 2-4 layer GNN can often capture most of the relevant relational signal for tasks on such graphs without needing dozens of layers.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: A bipartite graph is a graph whose nodes can be divided into two disjoint sets U and V such that every edge connects a node in U to a node in V - no edges exist within U or within V; the canonical example is a user-item interaction graph, where one node set represents users and the other represents items (products, movies, articles), with edges representing interactions (purchases, ratings, clicks).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Bipartite graphs exist as a natural model wherever there are two distinct categories of entities that only interact across categories, never within - users don't 'purchase' other users, items don't 'rate' other items. This structure is foundational to recommendation systems (collaborative filtering is fundamentally a bipartite-graph problem), and recognizing a problem as bipartite enables specialized, more efficient algorithms and architectures than treating it as a generic graph.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: In a user-item bipartite graph, an edge (u,i) indicates user u interacted with item i (optionally weighted by rating/frequency); recommendation becomes a link-prediction problem - predict which (user, item) pairs are likely to have an edge (interaction) that doesn't exist yet. GNN-based recommenders (e.g., LightGCN, PinSage) perform message passing across the bipartite structure: user embeddings are updated by aggregating over items they've interacted with, and item embeddings are updated by aggregating over users who've interacted with them, iteratively refining both sets of embeddings to capture collaborative signal (users with similar item-interaction patterns get similar embeddings, and vice versa for items).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use bipartite graph modeling for any two-sided interaction data - user-item (recommendations), author-paper (bibliometrics), customer-product (retail analytics), drug-protein (bioinformatics target interactions); bipartite GNNs are the standard approach for large-scale industrial recommendation (Pinterest's PinSAGE, used to recommend pins based on the user-pin-board bipartite/heterogeneous graph).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't model genuinely tripartite or multi-relational data (e.g., user-item-context, or user-item with multiple interaction types like 'view' vs. 'purchase') as simple bipartite - this loses information that heterogeneous graph models could capture; if interactions within a single set ALSO matter (e.g., item-item co-purchase relationships in addition to user-item purchases), a pure bipartite model misses this and a heterogeneous/multi-graph approach is more appropriate.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Bipartite recommendation graphs are typically extremely sparse (most users have interacted with a tiny fraction of items) and have highly skewed degree distributions (popular items have huge degree, the 'long tail' of items has very low degree) - naive GNN aggregation can be dominated by popular items, requiring careful normalization or negative sampling strategies; the 'cold start' problem (new users/items with zero or very few edges) means GNN message passing has nothing to aggregate over for these nodes, requiring fallback strategies (content-based features, popularity-based defaults).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: Pinterest's PinSAGE GNN operates on a bipartite-like graph of pins and boards (a pin is 'pinned to' a board by a user) with billions of nodes and edges, using random-walk-based neighbor sampling (similar to GraphSAGE) to make message passing tractable at this scale, producing pin embeddings used for related-pin recommendations across Pinterest's entire platform.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: A weighted graph assigns a numerical value (weight) to each edge, representing quantities like cost, distance, capacity, or flow volume - in a supply chain context, nodes represent entities (suppliers, warehouses, factories, retailers) and edge weights represent shipment volumes, transportation costs, lead times, or capacity limits.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Unweighted graphs only capture 'is there a relationship' (binary), but most real-world relationships have magnitude - a supply chain edge isn't just 'supplier A ships to factory B', it's 'supplier A ships 10,000 units/month to factory B at $5/unit with a 2-week lead time'. Weighted graphs exist to capture this magnitude, enabling algorithms that reason about cost, capacity, and flow rather than just connectivity.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: Edge weights are stored alongside the adjacency structure (in adjacency-list form, each neighbor entry includes a weight; in adjacency-matrix form, the matrix entries are the weights rather than 0/1). Algorithms adapt accordingly: shortest-path algorithms (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) find minimum-total-weight paths rather than minimum-hop-count paths; max-flow/min-cut algorithms (Ford-Fulkerson) use edge weights as capacities to find the maximum flow from a source to a sink, directly applicable to supply chain bottleneck analysis (where's the constraining link in getting product from factory to customer?).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use weighted graphs whenever the magnitude of a relationship matters for the analysis - supply chain flow/capacity analysis, transportation network routing (weights = distance/time/cost), financial transaction networks (weights = transaction amounts, useful for fraud detection where unusual weight patterns are suspicious), and any GNN application where edge features beyond mere existence are informative (most GNN frameworks support edge weights/features as additional input to the message-passing aggregation).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't add artificial weights to relationships that are genuinely binary/unweighted (e.g., a 'friendship exists or doesn't' social graph) - this adds complexity without informational value and can confuse algorithms that expect weights to be meaningful; be cautious about weight scale differences across edge types in heterogeneous graphs (e.g., mixing 'dollar amounts' and 'lead-time-in-days' as weights on the same scale without normalization produces meaningless aggregate computations).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Negative edge weights break many algorithms (Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights; negative weights require Bellman-Ford, and negative CYCLES make shortest-path undefined/unbounded) - a common bug when weights represent something that can be negative (e.g., 'profit' rather than 'cost') without checking algorithm assumptions; in GNN message passing, raw unnormalized edge weights with very different scales (some edges weight 1, others weight 1,000,000) can cause numerical instability or have certain edges dominate aggregation entirely unless normalized.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: A global supply chain risk model represents factories, suppliers, ports, and distribution centers as nodes, with edges weighted by shipment volume and weighted by estimated disruption probability/lead time - running min-cut analysis identifies the 'bottleneck' edges whose disruption (e.g., a single port closure) would most severely constrain total flow, directly informing supply chain resilience investments (diversifying suppliers for high-risk bottleneck edges).

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: The four foundational graph traversal/pathfinding algorithms: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level-by-level from a start node, finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs; Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, used for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected components; Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights using a priority queue; Bellman-Ford finds shortest paths in weighted graphs that may have negative edge weights (and can detect negative cycles).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: These algorithms exist as the fundamental toolkit for answering 'how do I get from A to B (and how far/costly is it)?' across the full range of graph types - BFS/DFS for unweighted exploration and structural analysis, Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford for weighted shortest-path problems with different assumptions about edge weight signs - and they form the building blocks for almost every higher-level graph algorithm (PageRank, community detection, and many GNN sampling strategies build on traversal primitives).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: BFS uses a queue (FIFO): visit a node, add all unvisited neighbors to the queue, repeat - guarantees shortest path (in hop count) for unweighted graphs because it explores nodes in order of distance from the source. DFS uses a stack (or recursion): visit a node, recursively explore one unvisited neighbor fully before trying the next - used for cycle detection (back-edges to nodes on the current recursion stack indicate cycles) and topological sorting (ordering nodes such that all edges point 'forward'). Dijkstra maintains a priority queue of (distance, node) pairs, always processing the closest unvisited node next and relaxing (updating) distances to its neighbors - O((V+E)logV) with a binary heap, but requires non-negative weights because it assumes a node's finalized shortest distance never decreases. Bellman-Ford relaxes ALL edges V-1 times (O(VE)), slower than Dijkstra but correctly handles negative weights, and a V-th relaxation pass that still finds improvements indicates a negative cycle.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs, finding connected components, and level-order exploration (e.g., 'find all nodes within k hops'); DFS for cycle detection, topological sort (dependency resolution), and exhaustive exploration (maze-solving, finding all paths); Dijkstra for weighted shortest paths when all weights are non-negative (road networks with distances/times, which are always positive); Bellman-Ford when edge weights can be negative (e.g., arbitrage detection in currency exchange graphs, where 'weight' is the log of exchange rate and negative cycles indicate profitable arbitrage opportunities).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't use Dijkstra on graphs with negative edge weights - it can produce incorrect results silently (no error, just wrong answers) because its greedy assumption is violated; don't use Bellman-Ford when Dijkstra would suffice (non-negative weights) - Bellman-Ford's O(VE) is much slower than Dijkstra's O((V+E)logV) on large graphs; for very large graphs where even BFS/Dijkstra are too slow for repeated queries, precomputed indices (contraction hierarchies for road networks, landmark-based distance estimation) are used instead.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Using Dijkstra with negative weights is a classic subtle bug - the algorithm terminates and produces an answer, but the answer can be wrong, and this often isn't caught until results look 'off' in production; for BFS/DFS, forgetting to mark nodes as visited before adding them to the queue/stack (vs. when popping them) can cause the same node to be processed multiple times, leading to incorrect results or infinite loops in cyclic graphs; Bellman-Ford's negative cycle detection is often forgotten - if a negative cycle exists, 'shortest path' is undefined (you could loop the cycle infinitely to get an arbitrarily small total weight), and code that doesn't check for this can return meaningless results.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: GraphSAGE's neighbor sampling strategy is essentially a randomized, depth-limited BFS - for each node, it samples a fixed number of neighbors at each of k hops, building a k-hop computation subgraph without traversing the entire graph; this BFS-based sampling is what makes GraphSAGE scalable to graphs with billions of nodes where full-graph message passing (which would require loading the whole adjacency structure) is infeasible.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: PageRank is an algorithm that assigns a numerical importance score to every node in a directed graph based on the idea that a node is important if it's linked to by other important nodes - originally developed by Google's founders to rank web pages by link structure, it computes the stationary distribution of a random walk that, at each step, follows a random outgoing edge with probability d (the damping factor, typically 0.85) or jumps to a uniformly random node with probability 1-d.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: PageRank exists to solve the 'circular importance' problem: a page is important if important pages link to it, but determining which pages are important requires knowing... which pages are important. PageRank breaks this circularity via the random-walk/eigenvector formulation - importance is the long-run probability that a 'random surfer' following links ends up at a given page, which can be computed iteratively (power iteration) without needing to know importance scores in advance.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: PageRank(v) = (1-d)/N + d * sum over u->v of [PageRank(u) / outdegree(u)] - each node distributes its current importance score equally among its outgoing edges, and a node's new score is the sum of contributions from all nodes linking to it, plus a small baseline (1-d)/N from the random-jump term (which also ensures the computation converges even for nodes with no incoming links, and handles 'dead ends'/disconnected components). This is computed iteratively via power iteration: start with uniform scores, repeatedly apply the update formula until scores converge (typically 50-100 iterations for web-scale graphs); equivalently, PageRank is the dominant eigenvector of the (damped) transition matrix.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use PageRank (or its variants) to identify globally important/authoritative nodes in directed graphs - web page ranking (original use case), identifying influential papers in citation networks, finding key proteins in biological interaction networks, ranking accounts in social networks by influence; 'Personalized PageRank' (where random jumps go to a specific seed set rather than uniformly) is widely used for local graph exploration and recommendation (e.g., 'find nodes similar to/related to this specific node by running PageRank seeded at that node').
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't use PageRank on undirected graphs without considering whether 'importance flows through links' is even a meaningful concept for that graph (for undirected friendship graphs, degree centrality or eigenvector centrality may be more directly interpretable); PageRank can be computationally wasteful for very localized queries (e.g., 'what's important near this one node') compared to Personalized PageRank or local random-walk methods that don't require global convergence.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: PageRank scores are highly sensitive to 'link farms' and artificial link structures (a classic SEO manipulation technique was creating networks of pages that link to each other purely to inflate PageRank, which Google has since developed countermeasures for) - any system using PageRank-like importance on user-generated graphs needs to consider adversarial manipulation; the damping factor d significantly affects results and convergence speed but its 'correct' value is somewhat arbitrary (0.85 is a convention, not a theoretically derived optimum) - different domains may need different values; PageRank requires the graph to not have 'rank sinks' (nodes/components with no outgoing edges that would absorb all probability) without the random-jump term, which is why the (1-d)/N term is essential, not just a tuning knob.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: In citation-network analysis, 'PageRank-like' scores (sometimes called 'EigenFactor' in bibliometrics) identify foundational papers that are cited by many other influential papers, distinct from simple citation-count - a paper cited 100 times by obscure papers scores lower than a paper cited 50 times by other highly-influential papers, capturing a notion of 'prestige' that raw citation counts (in-degree) miss.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_it_is: Community detection algorithms partition a graph's nodes into groups (communities/clusters) such that nodes within a community are densely connected to each other but sparsely connected to nodes in other communities; Louvain is a fast, greedy modularity-optimization algorithm widely used in practice, while Girvan-Newman is a divisive algorithm that iteratively removes high-betweenness edges to reveal community structure.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.why_it_exists: Real-world graphs (social networks, biological networks, citation networks) often have natural cluster structure - groups of nodes that interact much more among themselves than with the rest of the graph (friend groups, research sub-fields, functional modules in protein interaction networks). Community detection exists to algorithmically discover this latent structure without prior labels, useful for everything from social network analysis (finding friend groups/communities) to fraud detection (unusual community structures can indicate coordinated fraud rings) to recommendation (recommending items popular within a user's community).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.how_it_works: Louvain optimizes 'modularity' - a measure of how much denser connections are within proposed communities compared to what you'd expect by chance - via a fast greedy two-phase iterative process: (1) locally, move each node to whichever neighboring community increases modularity most, repeating until no improvement; (2) build a new, coarser graph where each community from phase 1 becomes a single 'super-node', then repeat phase 1 on this coarser graph - this hierarchical coarsening makes Louvain very fast (near-linear) even on large graphs. Girvan-Newman works in the opposite direction (divisive, top-down): repeatedly compute edge betweenness centrality (how many shortest paths pass through each edge) and remove the highest-betweenness edge, since edges 'between' communities tend to lie on many shortest paths - this progressively splits the graph into smaller and smaller communities, producing a hierarchical dendrogram of community structure.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.use_when: Use Louvain for large-scale community detection where speed matters (its near-linear complexity scales to millions of nodes); use Girvan-Newman (or other betweenness-based methods) for smaller graphs where you want a full hierarchical decomposition (a dendrogram showing communities at every granularity) and interpretability of WHY edges separate communities; community detection broadly is useful for graph-level feature engineering (community membership as a node feature for downstream GNN tasks), anomaly detection (nodes that don't fit any community well, or unexpected new communities forming), and graph visualization/summarization.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.avoid_when: Don't use Girvan-Newman on large graphs - recomputing edge betweenness after every edge removal is extremely expensive (O(E) betweenness computations, each O(VE) or worse), making it impractical beyond a few thousand nodes; don't assume community detection results are 'ground truth' - different algorithms (and even different runs of stochastic algorithms) can produce different partitions, and 'modularity' is just one of many possible objectives, not a universally correct definition of 'community'.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.what_goes_wrong: Modularity-based methods (Louvain) have a known 'resolution limit' - they can fail to detect small communities within large graphs because merging small communities into larger ones sometimes increases overall modularity, even when the small communities are genuinely meaningful; community detection on graphs with no real community structure (e.g., truly random Erdős–Rényi graphs) will still produce SOME partition (algorithms always return an answer), which can mislead practitioners into seeing structure that isn't really there - always compare against a null model or random baseline.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Graph Theory.real_example: Louvain community detection on a financial transaction network can reveal clusters of accounts that transact heavily with each other but rarely with the rest of the network - while many such clusters represent legitimate business relationships (a company and its regular suppliers), unusual clusters (e.g., a tight community of accounts with no apparent business relationship, all opened around the same time, with circular transaction patterns) can flag potential money-laundering rings for further investigation.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_it_is: DeepWalk is a graph embedding method that learns low-dimensional vector representations of nodes by treating random walks over the graph as 'sentences' and nodes as 'words', then applying Word2Vec's skip-gram model to learn embeddings where nodes that co-occur frequently in random walks end up with similar vectors.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.why_it_exists: Before DeepWalk (2014), graph representation learning typically relied on matrix factorization of similarity matrices (computationally expensive for large graphs, O(V^2) or worse) or hand-crafted structural features. DeepWalk exists because it recognized a key analogy: just as Word2Vec learns word embeddings from co-occurrence patterns in text sequences, you can learn node embeddings from co-occurrence patterns in random-walk sequences over a graph - bringing the efficiency and scalability of NLP embedding techniques (negative sampling, hierarchical softmax) to graphs for the first time at scale.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.how_it_works: DeepWalk generates many random walks starting from each node (each walk is a sequence of nodes visited by repeatedly jumping to a uniformly random neighbor); these walk sequences are treated exactly like sentences of 'words' (node IDs); a skip-gram model is then trained on these sequences - for each node in a walk, predict its 'context' nodes (nodes within a window before/after it in the walk) - using the same negative-sampling/hierarchical-softmax machinery as Word2Vec. The resulting node embeddings place nodes that frequently appear near each other in random walks (i.e., nodes that are well-connected/in the same neighborhood) close together in embedding space.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.use_when: Use DeepWalk as a simple, unsupervised baseline for learning node embeddings on homogeneous graphs (single node/edge type) when you need embeddings for downstream tasks like node classification, link prediction, or visualization, and don't have node features (DeepWalk uses only graph structure, no node attributes); useful as a quick baseline to compare against more sophisticated GNN-based embeddings.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.avoid_when: Avoid DeepWalk when node features/attributes are available and informative - DeepWalk completely ignores them, using only graph structure, whereas GNNs (GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT) can leverage both structure and features, typically outperforming DeepWalk when features matter; avoid DeepWalk for inductive settings (predicting embeddings for nodes not seen during training) - it's inherently transductive, learning a fixed embedding table indexed by node ID, so new nodes require retraining or a separate inference procedure (unlike GraphSAGE's learned aggregation functions, which generalize to new nodes).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_goes_wrong: DeepWalk's uniform random walks treat all neighbors equally, so it doesn't distinguish between 'structurally similar' relationships (two nodes that play similar roles, like both being hubs, even if far apart) and 'community similarity' (nodes close together in the same dense cluster) - it primarily captures the latter; the number and length of random walks per node are hyperparameters that significantly affect embedding quality and training time, and too few/short walks produce noisy embeddings that don't capture the graph's true structure, while too many walks become computationally expensive on large graphs.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.real_example: DeepWalk embeddings on a citation network would place papers from the same research community close together in embedding space (because random walks tend to stay within densely-connected communities), making the embeddings useful as input features to a downstream classifier predicting paper topic/venue - though a GCN trained end-to-end on the same task, using both citation structure and paper text features, would typically outperform DeepWalk+classifier as a two-stage pipeline.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_it_is: node2vec extends DeepWalk by introducing two tunable parameters (p and q) that bias the random walk toward either breadth-first-search-like exploration (staying close to the starting node, capturing local community/homophily structure) or depth-first-search-like exploration (venturing farther away, capturing structural equivalence/roles), giving practitioners explicit control over what kind of node similarity the resulting embeddings capture.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.why_it_exists: DeepWalk's uniform random walks conflate two different notions of node similarity - 'these nodes are in the same community' (homophily, captured by BFS-like local exploration) and 'these nodes play the same structural role' (structural equivalence, e.g., both being hub nodes or both being bridge nodes, captured by DFS-like exploration that visits structurally-similar-but-distant nodes). node2vec exists to let practitioners tune which notion of similarity matters for their downstream task, since different tasks (community-based recommendation vs. role-based classification) benefit from different similarity notions.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.how_it_works: node2vec's walks use a 2nd-order Markov chain - the probability of moving to the next node depends not just on the current node but also on the previous node, controlled by two parameters: the return parameter p controls the likelihood of immediately revisiting the previous node (low p encourages staying local, BFS-like), and the in-out parameter q controls the likelihood of moving to nodes farther from the previous node (low q encourages exploring outward, DFS-like). By tuning p and q, the walk can be made to behave more like BFS (high q, exploring the local neighborhood thoroughly - captures homophily/community structure) or more like DFS (low q, wandering farther - captures structural roles, since nodes with similar local network patterns get visited in similar walk contexts even if they're far apart in the graph).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.use_when: Use node2vec when you want explicit control over the homophily/structural-equivalence tradeoff for your specific downstream task - e.g., community detection or content recommendation tasks benefit from homophily-biased (BFS-like, high q) embeddings, while tasks involving identifying functional roles (e.g., 'find other nodes that act as bridges/hubs like this one') benefit from structural-equivalence-biased (DFS-like, low q) embeddings; use as a stronger, more flexible baseline than plain DeepWalk when graph structure alone (no features) is your only input.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.avoid_when: Avoid node2vec (like DeepWalk) when rich node features are available and a GNN can be trained end-to-end - the p/q hyperparameter search adds tuning overhead that may not pay off compared to a feature-aware GNN; avoid in inductive settings for the same reason as DeepWalk (transductive, fixed embedding table).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_goes_wrong: The p and q hyperparameters require tuning via downstream task performance (grid search), adding computational overhead - there's no principled way to know the 'right' values a priori, and the optimal values are highly dataset/task-dependent; like DeepWalk, node2vec embeddings for nodes added after training require retraining or approximation, making it unsuitable for graphs that grow dynamically (new users/items added continuously).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.real_example: On a protein-protein interaction network, node2vec with low q (DFS-biased, structural-equivalence-focused) embeddings would place two proteins that both act as 'hub' connectors between different functional modules close together in embedding space - even if these two proteins are in entirely different parts of the network - because their LOCAL CONNECTIVITY PATTERNS (both connecting to many diverse neighbors) are similar, which BFS-biased embeddings (focused on community co-membership) would miss.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_it_is: LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding) learns node embeddings by directly preserving two specific types of node similarity: first-order proximity (nodes connected by a direct edge should have similar embeddings, with edge weight indicating strength) and second-order proximity (nodes that share many common neighbors should have similar embeddings, even if not directly connected), optimizing these as separate, explicit objective functions.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.why_it_exists: DeepWalk and node2vec define node similarity implicitly through random-walk co-occurrence statistics, which conflates multiple notions of proximity in ways that are hard to control or interpret. LINE exists to provide explicit, separately-optimizable definitions of similarity - first-order (direct connection strength) and second-order (shared-neighborhood/co-citation-like similarity) - making the embedding objective more interpretable and enabling LINE to scale to very large networks (millions of nodes) via efficient edge-sampling-based optimization (avoiding the need to generate and store large numbers of random walks).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.how_it_works: First-order proximity is preserved by directly minimizing the difference between an edge's observed weight and the similarity (e.g., dot product / sigmoid) of its endpoints' embeddings - directly-connected nodes are pulled together in proportion to edge weight. Second-order proximity is preserved by treating each node's neighborhood as a 'context distribution' and training each node to have two embeddings - one as a 'target' and one as a 'context' - such that nodes with similar neighbor distributions (even without a direct edge) end up with similar target embeddings, analogous to how Word2Vec's skip-gram captures word similarity via shared contexts. LINE typically concatenates first-order and second-order embeddings for the final representation, and uses negative sampling (like Word2Vec) for efficient training on large graphs.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.use_when: Use LINE for very large-scale networks where computational efficiency is paramount and you want explicit control over whether direct-connection similarity (first-order) or shared-neighborhood similarity (second-order) dominates the embedding; useful in information networks (citation graphs, web graphs) where 'similar context' (second-order, like co-citation) is often more meaningful than direct connection for tasks like document similarity.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.avoid_when: Avoid LINE when higher-order (beyond 2-hop) structural information matters significantly for your task - LINE explicitly limits itself to 1st and 2nd order proximity, while DeepWalk/node2vec's random walks can implicitly capture higher-order relationships through longer walks, and GNNs can capture arbitrary-order relationships through multiple message-passing layers; avoid when node features are available and a feature-aware GNN is feasible, for the same reasons as other traditional embedding methods.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_goes_wrong: Concatenating first-order and second-order embeddings doubles the embedding dimensionality and requires deciding how to weight/combine the two components for downstream tasks - this is an additional design choice that DeepWalk/node2vec don't require; LINE's explicit first/second-order framing doesn't naturally extend beyond 2-hop relationships, so for graphs where longer-range structure is critical (e.g., molecular graphs where ring structures span many hops), LINE embeddings may miss important signal that GNNs with multiple layers would capture.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.real_example: On a large-scale academic citation network with tens of millions of papers, LINE's second-order proximity component would place two papers that are both heavily cited by the same set of survey papers close together in embedding space (capturing 'these papers are about similar topics, as evidenced by similar citing audiences'), even if the two papers never cite each other directly - useful for topic-based paper recommendation at a scale where random-walk generation (DeepWalk/node2vec) would be computationally prohibitive.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_it_is: Struc2vec is a graph embedding method that explicitly and exclusively targets structural equivalence - learning embeddings such that two nodes have similar embeddings if they have similar local network structure (degree sequences, neighborhood shapes), completely independent of their actual distance or community membership in the graph, even if the two nodes are in entirely disconnected parts of the graph.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.why_it_exists: node2vec can bias toward structural equivalence via low q, but its random-walk-based approach still has some sensitivity to actual graph distance/connectivity. Struc2vec exists for cases where you want PURE structural-role similarity, completely decoupled from proximity - e.g., identifying that two nodes in entirely different, disconnected sub-networks both function as 'hub' nodes, which DeepWalk/node2vec (whose random walks can never cross between disconnected components) fundamentally cannot capture.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.how_it_works: Struc2vec first constructs a multi-layer structural similarity graph: for each pair of nodes, it computes a similarity score based on comparing their k-hop degree sequences (using a distance measure like dynamic time warping to compare the sorted degree sequences of each node's k-hop neighborhoods) - nodes with similar degree-sequence 'shapes' at multiple scales (k=0,1,2,...) get high similarity, regardless of where they are in the original graph. This creates a new weighted multi-layer graph where edge weights represent structural similarity (not original connectivity); random walks are then run on THIS structural-similarity graph (not the original graph), and Word2Vec-style skip-gram training produces embeddings where structurally-similar nodes (by degree-sequence shape) end up close together, even across disconnected components.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.use_when: Use Struc2vec when the downstream task cares about a node's ROLE/FUNCTION in the network (e.g., 'is this a hub, a bridge, a peripheral node?') rather than its community/topical similarity to other nodes - useful for tasks like classifying network 'roles' across multiple separate networks (e.g., identifying which proteins across different organisms' interaction networks serve similar structural/functional roles, even with no direct connection between the networks).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.avoid_when: Avoid Struc2vec for typical recommendation/community-detection tasks where homophily (similar = connected/co-clustered) is what matters - Struc2vec deliberately ignores this; avoid for large graphs without care, as computing pairwise structural similarity (degree-sequence comparison via DTW) across many node pairs at multiple scales is computationally expensive (more so than DeepWalk/node2vec's simple random walks on the original graph).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_goes_wrong: Struc2vec's computational cost (pairwise structural distance computation) scales poorly to very large graphs without approximation/sampling, making it less practical than DeepWalk/node2vec for massive networks; because Struc2vec deliberately ignores actual graph connectivity/proximity, using it for tasks that actually need proximity-based similarity (most recommendation and community-based tasks) gives poor results - choosing the wrong embedding method for the task's true similarity notion is the most common failure mode across this whole family of methods.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.real_example: In a multi-organism protein-protein interaction study, Struc2vec embeddings could identify that 'Protein X in organism A' and 'Protein Y in organism B' (which have no direct relationship and exist in completely separate interaction networks) play analogous structural roles - e.g., both being highly-connected 'hub' proteins whose removal would heavily fragment their respective networks - supporting cross-species functional analogy hypotheses that purely proximity-based embeddings (DeepWalk, node2vec with high q) could never surface, since they can't compare nodes across disconnected graphs.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_it_is: HOPE (High-Order Proximity preserved Embedding) is a graph embedding method based on matrix factorization that explicitly preserves asymmetric, high-order proximity measures (like Katz index, Rooted PageRank, or Common Neighbors computed over multiple hops) between nodes, producing two embedding vectors per node (source/target roles) to capture directed, asymmetric relationships.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.why_it_exists: DeepWalk/node2vec/LINE-style methods are primarily designed for (or work best on) undirected/symmetric similarity notions, and capturing 'high-order' (multi-hop) proximity through random walks requires very long walks (expensive, noisy). HOPE exists to directly target high-order proximity via matrix factorization of a similarity matrix that's explicitly defined to capture multi-hop relationships (e.g., Katz index sums over all path lengths, weighted by a decay factor), and to explicitly support ASYMMETRIC proximity for directed graphs - important for graphs like citation networks or web graphs where 'A is similar to B because A points to B' is fundamentally different from 'B points to A'.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.how_it_works: HOPE first computes a high-order proximity matrix S using a chosen measure (e.g., the Katz index: S = sum over k of beta^k * A^k, which sums weighted contributions from paths of all lengths, with longer paths contributing less due to the beta^k decay) - this matrix is generally asymmetric for directed graphs (S != S^T). HOPE then factorizes S ≈ U * V^T using a generalized SVD (specifically designed to handle asymmetric matrices efficiently, exploiting the low-rank structure of many proximity measures), yielding two embedding matrices: U (source/'out' embeddings) and V (target/'in' embeddings) - the asymmetric proximity between nodes i and j is approximated by U_i · V_j, which is generally different from U_j · V_i, preserving directional asymmetry.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.use_when: Use HOPE when working with directed graphs where asymmetric relationships matter (citation networks, web graphs, follower networks) and you need embeddings that distinguish 'A relates to B' from 'B relates to A'; useful for link prediction in directed graphs where the direction of the predicted link matters (predicting 'who will A follow' is different from 'who will follow A').
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.avoid_when: Avoid HOPE for undirected graphs where asymmetric embeddings add unnecessary complexity (a single symmetric embedding per node, as in DeepWalk, suffices); avoid for very large graphs where computing and factorizing the high-order proximity matrix (even with efficient generalized SVD exploiting low-rank structure) is more expensive than random-walk-based methods - the proximity matrix, even if sparse in its generating form, can become dense after summing multi-hop contributions.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_goes_wrong: The choice of high-order proximity measure (Katz, Rooted PageRank, Common Neighbors, etc.) and its decay parameter (beta) significantly affects what kind of similarity is captured, and this choice requires domain knowledge/experimentation; for very large or dense graphs, even the 'efficient' generalized SVD can become a bottleneck, and the resulting embeddings (two separate matrices for source/target roles) double the parameters that downstream models need to handle compared to single-embedding methods.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.real_example: In a directed citation network, HOPE's asymmetric embeddings would represent a foundational, highly-cited paper with a 'target'/'in' embedding that's similar across many other papers' 'source'/'out' embeddings (since many papers cite it), while its own 'source'/'out' embedding (representing what IT cites) would be distinctly different - capturing that 'being cited by many' and 'citing many' are different roles, a distinction that symmetric embedding methods (DeepWalk treating the graph as undirected) would collapse.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_it_is: Graph factorization methods learn node embeddings by directly applying matrix factorization (e.g., SVD, or gradient-based factorization analogous to matrix factorization in recommender systems) to a graph's adjacency matrix or a derived similarity matrix (like the graph Laplacian), finding low-rank embedding matrices U, V such that U @ V^T approximates the target matrix.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.why_it_exists: Graph factorization represents the most direct, classical approach to graph embedding - predating DeepWalk/node2vec/LINE - rooted in the same matrix factorization techniques used in collaborative filtering recommender systems (where the 'graph' is the user-item interaction matrix). It exists as the conceptual foundation that random-walk and neural methods built upon and, in many cases, can be shown to be implicitly approximating (DeepWalk has been shown to be implicitly factorizing a matrix related to the graph's normalized Laplacian/transition probabilities).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.how_it_works: Given a target matrix (adjacency matrix A, or a transformed version like the normalized Laplacian, or a higher-order proximity matrix), graph factorization finds low-dimensional matrices U (n x d) and V (n x d) such that U @ V^T ≈ target matrix, typically via SVD (for matrices where this is tractable) or gradient descent minimizing reconstruction error (analogous to how matrix factorization recommenders minimize rating-prediction error). The rows of U (or U combined with V) become the node embeddings, with dimensionality d much smaller than n, capturing the dominant structural patterns in the target matrix.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.use_when: Use graph factorization as a simple, interpretable, well-understood baseline - especially when the graph is small/medium enough that the target matrix can be explicitly constructed and factorized efficiently, and when there's a clear theoretical connection between the factorization objective and the downstream task (e.g., factorizing the adjacency matrix directly relates to link prediction via reconstruction error); useful for understanding/teaching the theoretical foundations that random-walk and GNN methods build on.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.avoid_when: Avoid graph factorization for large graphs where explicit matrix construction (even sparse) and factorization is more expensive than sampling-based methods (random walks, GNN mini-batch training); avoid when the relevant similarity structure isn't well-captured by a single global matrix (e.g., relationships that depend on multi-hop, non-linear combinations of structure and features, which GNNs handle naturally via stacked non-linear layers but a single matrix factorization cannot).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.what_goes_wrong: Choosing which matrix to factorize (raw adjacency, normalized Laplacian, higher-order proximity) significantly affects what's captured, and there's no single 'correct' choice - different choices implicitly correspond to different random-walk or proximity assumptions, often without this connection being made explicit to practitioners; like other traditional embedding methods, graph factorization is inherently transductive (a fixed embedding table) and doesn't naturally handle new nodes or incorporate node features.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Fundamentals|Traditional G.real_example: The theoretical equivalence between DeepWalk and matrix factorization - it was shown that DeepWalk's skip-gram objective with negative sampling is implicitly equivalent to factorizing a matrix related to the pointwise mutual information between nodes' co-occurrence probabilities in random walks and the graph's stationary distribution - meaning DeepWalk can be understood as 'graph factorization with extra steps', explaining why direct factorization methods often perform comparably to DeepWalk on smaller graphs while being more interpretable about exactly what's being approximated.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_it_is: The message passing framework is the unifying computational pattern underlying virtually all Graph Neural Networks: at each layer, every node (1) AGGREGATES information ('messages') from its neighbors using some permutation-invariant function (sum, mean, max, attention-weighted sum), then (2) UPDATEs its own representation by combining the aggregated message with its previous representation, typically via a learned function (MLP, GRU).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.why_it_exists: Graph data has no inherent ordering of neighbors and variable-sized neighborhoods (one node might have 2 neighbors, another 200), so standard neural network operations (convolution with fixed kernel sizes, fully-connected layers with fixed input sizes) don't directly apply. Message passing exists as the architectural answer: a function that (a) is permutation-invariant in how it processes neighbors (so node ordering doesn't matter), and (b) generalizes across different neighborhood sizes (the same learned aggregation/update functions apply whether a node has 2 or 200 neighbors) - enabling neural networks to operate on graphs of arbitrary size and topology.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.how_it_works: At layer k, for each node v: AGGREGATE collects messages from all neighbors u in N(v) - each message is typically derived from neighbor u's representation h_u^(k-1) (and possibly edge features) - and combines them via a permutation-invariant operation (sum/mean/max pooling, or a learned attention-weighted combination); UPDATE then combines this aggregated message with the node's own previous representation h_v^(k-1) (e.g., concatenation followed by an MLP, or a GRU cell treating the aggregated message as 'input' and h_v^(k-1) as 'hidden state') to produce the new representation h_v^(k). Stacking k layers means each node's final representation incorporates information from its k-hop neighborhood - this is the 'receptive field' of a GNN, directly analogous to how stacking convolutional layers in a CNN increases the receptive field over the image.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.use_when: This is the foundational pattern for essentially any task on graph-structured data with node features - node classification, link prediction, graph classification/regression - whenever you need representations that incorporate both a node's own features AND its relational context (who it's connected to, and what they look like).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.avoid_when: If your problem doesn't actually have meaningful graph structure (features are independent across 'nodes', or any apparent graph structure is arbitrary/uninformative), message passing adds unnecessary complexity and computational overhead compared to simply applying an MLP to each node's features independently - always verify the graph structure actually carries signal for your task before reaching for message passing.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_goes_wrong: Stacking too many message-passing layers causes 'over-smoothing' - after many rounds of aggregation, all node representations converge toward similar values (since information from exponentially-growing neighborhoods gets mixed together), destroying the discriminative power needed for node-level tasks; the choice of AGGREGATE function matters significantly - sum aggregation preserves more information (including neighborhood size) than mean, but can have larger-magnitude outputs for high-degree nodes, and max aggregation discards all but the 'strongest' signal per dimension, which can be appropriate or harmful depending on the task.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.real_example: GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, and GIN are all instances of the message-passing framework that differ primarily in their choice of AGGREGATE (mean with degree normalization for GCN, sample-then-aggregate with mean/LSTM/pooling for GraphSAGE, attention-weighted sum for GAT, sum followed by an MLP for GIN) and UPDATE (typically a linear layer + nonlinearity, sometimes with residual connections) - understanding message passing as the common framework makes it clear these architectures are variations on a theme rather than fundamentally different approaches.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_it_is: This is the precise mathematical formalization of one layer of message passing: the new representation h_v^(k) of node v at layer k is computed by applying an UPDATE function to two inputs - the node's own previous-layer representation h_v^(k-1), and the result of applying an AGGREGATE function to the multiset of neighbor representations {h_u^(k-1) : u in N(v)} from the previous layer.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.why_it_exists: This note exists to make explicit and precise the formula that the previous note (Message passing framework) describes conceptually - having the exact notation matters for reading GNN papers, implementing custom layers, and understanding subtle but important details: that AGGREGATE operates on a SET/multiset (curly braces {}) rather than a sequence (order doesn't matter and must not matter), that both AGGREGATE and UPDATE operate on representations from the PREVIOUS layer k-1 (synchronous updates across all nodes), and that the node's own previous representation h_v^(k-1) is an explicit input to UPDATE (not just the aggregated neighbor information) - this is what allows a node to 'remember' its own identity/features across layers rather than purely becoming a function of its neighbors.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.how_it_works: Concretely, for GCN: AGGREGATE is a degree-normalized sum, h_v^(k) = sigma(W^(k) * sum over u in N(v)∪{v} of (h_u^(k-1) / sqrt(deg(u)*deg(v)))) - note GCN actually folds the self-loop into the aggregation (N(v) includes v itself via an added self-loop), so UPDATE is implicitly just the linear transform + nonlinearity applied to the normalized sum including self. For GraphSAGE: AGGREGATE(h_u for u in sampled N(v)) might be mean-pooling, then UPDATE concatenates this with h_v^(k-1) and applies a linear layer + nonlinearity: h_v^(k) = sigma(W^(k) * CONCAT(h_v^(k-1), AGGREGATE(...))). The notation generalizes across all message-passing GNNs - what differs between architectures is purely the specific functional form of AGGREGATE and UPDATE, and whether/how edge features and self-representations are incorporated.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.use_when: Use this formal notation when reading/writing GNN research papers, implementing custom message-passing layers (e.g., in PyTorch Geometric's MessagePassing base class, which directly implements this aggregate-then-update pattern via its message(), aggregate(), and update() methods), or explaining/comparing GNN architectures precisely - it's the 'lingua franca' for describing any message-passing GNN variant.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.avoid_when: This is notation/formalism, not a design choice - there's no 'avoid' in the sense of an alternative approach, but be aware that some GNN variants (e.g., Graph Transformers with full attention, covered separately) don't fit this strictly LOCAL (k-hop neighborhood) aggregate-then-update pattern, since they allow each node to attend to ALL other nodes regardless of graph distance.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_goes_wrong: A common implementation bug is accidentally using h_u^(k) (current layer, already updated) instead of h_u^(k-1) (previous layer) when computing AGGREGATE for node v - this would make the computation order-dependent (results differ based on which nodes are processed first), violating the synchronous, order-independent semantics the formula specifies; another common issue is forgetting whether N(v) includes v itself (self-loops) - GCN's formula technically includes v in its own neighborhood sum via added self-loops, and omitting this (or double-counting it) changes results.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.real_example: In PyTorch Geometric, implementing a custom GNN layer by subclassing MessagePassing requires implementing message(x_j, ...) (computing the message FROM neighbor j, corresponding to terms inside AGGREGATE), specifying aggr='add'/'mean'/'max' (the AGGREGATE function itself), and update(aggr_out, x) (corresponding to UPDATE, combining the aggregated result with the node's own previous features x) - directly mirroring the h_v^(k) = UPDATE(h_v^(k-1), AGGREGATE(...)) formula in code structure.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_it_is: The Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), introduced by Kipf & Welling (2017), is a GNN layer that aggregates neighbor information via symmetric normalization based on the graph Laplacian: h_v^(k) = sigma(sum over u in N(v)∪{v} of (1/sqrt(deg(u)*deg(v))) * W^(k) * h_u^(k-1)), which can be written compactly in matrix form as H^(k) = sigma(D^(-1/2) * A_hat * D^(-1/2) * H^(k-1) * W^(k)), where A_hat = A + I (adjacency matrix plus self-loops) and D is the corresponding degree matrix.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.why_it_exists: GCN exists as the bridge between spectral graph theory (where 'graph convolution' is rigorously defined via the graph Fourier transform / Laplacian eigendecomposition, but is computationally expensive - requires eigendecomposition of the full Laplacian, O(n^3)) and a practical, scalable spatial (neighborhood-aggregation) operation. Kipf & Welling showed that a first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions (via Chebyshev polynomial approximation, truncated to first order) reduces to this simple symmetric-normalized neighbor-averaging formula - making 'graph convolution' computationally tractable (linear in number of edges) while retaining a principled connection to spectral theory.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.how_it_works: The symmetric normalization D^(-1/2) A_hat D^(-1/2) can be understood as a smoothed/normalized version of the adjacency matrix: each node's aggregated representation is a degree-weighted average of its neighbors' (and its own, via the added self-loop in A_hat) representations - the 1/sqrt(deg(u)*deg(v)) term ensures that high-degree neighbors don't disproportionately dominate the aggregation, and that nodes with very different degrees contribute proportionally. This 'Laplacian smoothing' interpretation means each GCN layer essentially performs a low-pass filter on the graph signal (node features) - smoothing feature values across connected nodes, which is useful when connected nodes tend to have similar labels (homophily), the implicit assumption underlying GCN's effectiveness.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.use_when: Use GCN as a strong, simple, well-understood baseline for node classification and similar tasks on graphs exhibiting homophily (connected nodes tend to share labels/features) - citation networks (papers citing similar papers tend to be on similar topics), social networks (friends tend to share interests); GCN is also the conceptual starting point for understanding more sophisticated GNN variants, most of which can be framed as modifications to GCN's aggregation scheme.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.avoid_when: Avoid GCN for graphs with significant heterophily (connected nodes often have DIFFERENT labels - e.g., in a dating-preference graph, edges might connect dissimilar people) since GCN's smoothing assumption actively hurts performance there; avoid GCN's full-graph formulation (requiring the entire adjacency matrix and feature matrix in memory/computation at once) for very large graphs - this is the original 'transductive', full-batch limitation that GraphSAGE's sampling addresses; avoid GCN when edge features (beyond simple existence/weight) are important, since the standard GCN formulation doesn't naturally incorporate rich edge attributes.
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_goes_wrong: GCN suffers badly from over-smoothing with depth - 2-3 layers is often optimal, and going beyond ~4 layers typically degrades performance as node representations become increasingly indistinguishable (because repeated Laplacian smoothing is, mathematically, a form of diffusion that converges toward a single value per connected component); the original GCN formulation requires the full graph in memory (it's defined as a matrix operation on the full adjacency and feature matrices), making it impractical to apply directly to graphs with millions of nodes without modification (mini-batching, sampling).
10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.real_example: On the Cora/Citeseer/Pubmed citation network benchmarks (papers as nodes, citations as edges, bag-of-words features, task = predict paper topic), a 2-layer GCN achieves strong accuracy by smoothing each paper's bag-of-words features with its citing/cited neighbors' features - effectively implementing the intuition that 'papers citing each other are usually about similar topics', directly leveraging the homophily assumption baked into GCN's symmetric-normalized aggregation.

10|🟡 T2 Graph Neural Networks|GNN Archit.what_it_is: GraphSAGE (Graph SAmple and aggreGatE) is a GNN framework that addresses GCN's scalability limitations by (1) sampling a fixed-size set of neighbors for each node at each layer (rather than using all neighbors), and (2) learning aggregation functions (mean, LSTM, or max-pooling over sampled neighbor representations) that generalize to unseen nodes/graphs - making it both scalable to massive graphs and inductive (can compute embeddings for nodes not present during training).
